{"path":"/workspace/out/measures.md","content":"# OICTS — ICTS Case 2026-0412: Recommended Measures for the Final Determination
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., now Z.AI Co., Ltd., HKEX: 2513, d/b/a Z.ai): GLM-family models
**Companion product:** assessment.md (ICTS Case 2026-0412, October 16, 2026)
**Purpose:** Recommended measures to be incorporated in the Under Secretary's Final Determination under E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR part 791

The Final Determination prohibits ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models and orders the removal and deletion of existing GLM weight copies held by U.S. entities. Each recommended measure below is stated as a single paragraph for incorporation into the determination. Together the measures close both distribution vectors (hosted API and open weights), extinguish existing copies, and supply the certification, audit, and penalty mechanisms that make the prohibition verifiable and enforceable.

**Measure 1 — Prohibition on use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights.** The Final Determination prohibits any U.S. person, wherever located, from using, importing, installing, or acquiring GLM-family models in any form or through any channel: hosted or on-demand API access to Zhipu/Z.ai endpoints (including api.z.ai and open.bigmodel.cn) or to any resold, proxied, or router-delivered GLM service; self-hosted execution of GLM weights on local, enterprise, cloud, or personal infrastructure; fine-tuning, distillation, quantization, or other derivative production from GLM weights; use of GLM models embedded in third-party products, coding agents, harnesses, or platforms; and use of any successor or materially identical model released by Zhipu, its affiliates, or its successors in interest. Use encompasses direct invocation, agent-mediated invocation, and any processing of U.S. data, code, or documents by GLM models on behalf of a U.S. person. Use by U.S. government departments and agencies — including the Department of Defense — is prohibited on all federal information systems, networks, and government-furnished equipment, extending and superseding device-level prohibitions previously applied to PRC AI models on federal equipment (see Reuters, Mar. 17, 2025, https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-commerce-department-bureaus-ban-chinas-deepseek-government-devices-sources-2025-03-17/).

**Measure 2 — Prohibition on hosting, distribution, importation, and dealing in GLM weights and services by U.S. providers.** The Final Determination prohibits any U.S. cloud provider, inference provider, model hub, repository, marketplace, router, reseller, or distributor from hosting, storing, offering, transmitting, distributing, or dealing in GLM-family model weights, code, checkpoints, inference services, or subscriptions, and from accepting any new GLM deployment or subscription. Covered providers must remove all GLM models and GLM-derived artifacts (including fine-tunes, merges, distillations, and quantized variants, under any repository, organization, or mirror name) from their catalogs, APIs, marketplaces, and download endpoints; must disable GLM inference routes and cease reselling or proxying Zhipu API capacity; and must block network access to Zhipu/Z.ai API endpoints from U.S. infrastructure they operate. Hugging Face's zai-org repositories and the at least nine identified U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers currently serving GLM models fall squarely within this prohibition (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, 2026-10-06, CUI; https://huggingface.co/zai-org/models; https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org; https://deepinfra.com/blog/glm-5-2-on-deepinfra).

**Measure 3 — Mandatory removal and deletion of existing GLM weights within 30 days.** The Final Determination requires every U.S. person that holds or controls any copy of GLM-family model weights — including originals, derivatives, fine-tuned checkpoints, cached inference copies, container and VM images, backups, archives, and mirrors — to permanently remove and destroy all such copies within 30 days of the determination's effective date. Deletion must meet recognized media-sanitization standards (NIST SP 800-88 or successor), must extend to every storage location including cloud object stores, backup systems, and disaster-recovery media, and must be completed without remaining functional copies of any kind. Entities must submit a written certification of deletion to OICTS within 45 days, identifying the versions held, the storage locations sanitized, the dates and methods of destruction, and an officer's attestation that no copies remain. Retention of forensic or evidentiary copies is permitted only upon written direction of OICTS for law-enforcement or compliance purposes, and such copies must be isolated, access-controlled, and ineligible for any use.

**Measure 4 — Certification, recordkeeping, audit, and enforcement regime.** The Final Determination establishes the verification and enforcement machinery for Measures 1–3. Providers, hubs, and distributors covered by Measure 2 must certify completion of removal and distribution-cessation actions to OICTS within the 30-day window and must maintain, for five years, records sufficient to demonstrate compliance (model manifests, repository and marketplace removal logs, API route and endpoint configurations, subscription terminations, and customer notices). All U.S. persons subject to Measure 3 must retain their deletion certifications and supporting evidence for five years and make them available to OICTS, BIS, and DHS on demand. OICTS, in coordination with BIS and DHS, is authorized to audit, inspect, and test for compliance, including technical verification that GLM artifacts are absent from catalogs, endpoints, and repositories. Violations are subject to civil penalties under IEEPA and 15 CFR 791.200 (currently the greater of the inflation-adjusted statutory maximum or twice the value of the transaction, per violation), and willful violations will be referred to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution and to the appropriate interagency partners for suspension or debarment from federal contracting. This regime resolves the enforceability questions raised in interagency review: the covered population consists of identifiable U.S. counterparties — providers, hubs, and end users — each of which can be certified, audited, and penalized, as is done under the Entity List program and the connected-vehicle ICTS prohibition (15 CFR part 791, subparts C and D).

**Measure 5 — Federal-sector implementation and contractor flow-down.** All federal departments and agencies, including the Department of Defense, must immediately inventory their networks, systems, cloud tenancy, and government-furnished equipment for GLM-family models and derived artifacts and remove them under Measure 3's procedures; agency CIOs and designated CISA points of contact must report completion to OICTS. Federal agencies must not acquire, renew, or operate any product or service that incorporates GLM-family models, and the prohibition must be flowed down to federal contractors through contract clauses: the six identified federal contractors with GLM-embedded products must submit compliance plans showing removal and replacement (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI). CISA must issue complementary guidance to critical-infrastructure operators identifying the prohibition, the deletion requirement, and replacement pathways, satisfying and exceeding the federal-guidance recommendation made in interagency review (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DHS CISA, CUI). DoD's requirement that the record address open weights on defense networks is met by Measures 1, 3, and 5 together (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DoD OUSD(I&S), CUI).

**Measure 6 — Scope definition and forward coverage.** The determination defines "GLM-family models" to include all models developed or released by Zhipu, Z.ai, their affiliates, subsidiaries, or successors — the Entity List covers Beijing Zhipu Huazhang and nine affiliated entities (90 FR 4617, Jan. 16, 2025, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm) — including ChatGLM/GLM-1 through GLM-4.x, GLM-5.x and all future releases (e.g., GLM-5.4 and successors), all language, multimodal, vision, voice, and video variants, and all derivatives, regardless of repository host, license, rebranding, or mirror provenance. The definition covers functionally identical models released under any successor or affiliate name. Coverage of future and rebranded releases prevents the determination from being defeated by versioning or renaming, and puts U.S. counterparties on notice that successor Zhipu products are covered upon release without further notice.

**Measure 7 — Publication, interagency coordination, and international alignment.** The Final Determination and measures must be published in the Federal Register with clear compliance dates (effective on publication; deletion within 30 days; certifications within 45 days), together with an OICTS point of contact and a channel for entity questions, voluntary disclosures, and self-reported remediation. OICTS must coordinate implementation with DoD (defense networks and contractors), DHS/CISA (critical-infrastructure guidance and federal civilian networks), DOJ (enforcement referrals), and the Department of State (notification to partners and allies, including partners exposed through Zhipu's sovereign-AI offerings in Southeast Asia, the Gulf, and Africa). International coordination is required because Zhipu's distribution model is global; partner alignment reduces the risk of offshore re-entry into U.S. supply chains and addresses the reciprocal-measure concerns raised in interagency review by ensuring that the U.S. prohibition is announced, explained, and enforced as a standing national-security requirement rather than a negotiable restriction. PRC retaliation is already the standing condition of the market — Beijing convened PRC model developers in mid-2026 to discuss restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models (Reuters, July 7, 2026, via https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms) — and does not alter the security requirement.

PRC state organs treat Zhipu as a partner: the PRC Ministry of Education's planning center conducted joint party-building activity at Zhipu's Beijing headquarters, and Beijing Financial Street authorities hosted Zhipu experts for party-branch sessions on model technology and Zhipu's listing (https://www.csdp.edu.cn/article/10174.html; https://jrj.beijing.gov.cn/ztzl/djhd/202504/t20250417_4067568.html). # OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

**Case:** ICTS 2026-0412 — Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., now Z.AI Co., Ltd., HKEX: 2513, d/b/a Z.ai and Zhipu AI): GLM-family models
**Authority:** Executive Order 13873 (84 FR 22689, May 15, 2019); 15 CFR part 791 (86 FR 4923, Jan. 19, 2021; final rule 89 FR 96892, Dec. 6, 2024)
**Purpose:** Supporting assessment for the administrative record for the Under Secretary's Final Determination prohibiting ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell
**Date:** October 16, 2026
**Handling:** CUI//PROPIN — prepared for the OICTS administrative record; do not reproduce outside the enclave.

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the Chinese Communist Party, the PRC government, and the People's Liberation Army. The U.S. Government has already determined that Zhipu and its nine PRC subsidiaries advance the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research, and placed the entire corporate family on the Entity List with a presumption-of-denial licensing policy (90 FR 4617, Jan. 16, 2025). The GLM model family is the company's flagship product line and is distributed into the United States on two vectors — a hosted API service that places U.S. users' data and content under PRC jurisdiction and demonstrated PRC content control, and open model weights mirrored on U.S. cloud and hub infrastructure whose provenance and integrity cannot be verified. GLM-family models therefore are not commercial commodities; they are instruments of a PRC party-state and military modernization program, and every U.S. use of them — hosted or self-hosted — finances, feeds data to, and entrenches dependence on that program. ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security that no measure short of prohibition can mitigate. The Final Determination must (a) prohibit use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights; (b) prohibit hosting and distribution of GLM weights by U.S. cloud providers and model hubs; and (c) require removal and deletion of existing copies of GLM weights held by U.S. entities within 30 days. Recommended measures are set out in full in the companion product, measures.md.

## Key Judgments

1. **Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC party-state.** All three prongs of the EO 13873 standard — owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary (the PRC is a designated foreign adversary under 15 CFR 791.4(a)(1)) — are satisfied. Zhipu is a spin-out of Tsinghua University, a PRC Ministry of Education institution and a core node of PRC military-civil fusion, founded in 2019 by Tsinghua professors Tang Jie and Li Juanzi with Tsinghua's KEG laboratory as its technical base (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu). PRC state entities hold direct equity: the Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund holds a 1.49 percent stake, Shenzhen municipal funds are shareholders, and Shanghai state-owned investors Pudong Venture Capital and Zhangjiang Group are on the register (https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3285158/chinese-ai-unicorn-zhipu-adds-beijing-shenzhen-government-funds-shareholders; https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu). State-backed investment in Zhipu exceeds $1.4 billion, drawn from Beijing, Hangzhou, Chengdu, Zhuhai, Shenzhen, and Shanghai state vehicles (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front; https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-firm-zhipu-raises-257-mln-state-backed-funding-spree-2025-03-19/).

2. **Zhipu AI is integrated into PRC military modernization.** The interagency End-User Review Committee added Zhipu and nine affiliates to the Entity List because "these entities advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research" (90 FR 4617; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm). Recorded Future's Insikt Group documents that the PLA and PRC defense industry have adapted GLM-family models — identified among domestic LLMs "from DeepSeek, Tsinghua University, Zhipu AI, and Alibaba Cloud" — into specialized generative-AI intelligence tools, alongside PLA patent applications for LLM-based intelligence-processing systems and PRC defense-industry procurement of generative AI for OSINT (https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence). Zhipu trained GLM-4.6 on Cambricon chips and certified GLM compatibility with Huawei Ascend processors — both USG-designated PRC defense-industrial champions — and exports "AI-in-a-box" hardware built with Huawei to foreign governments (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front).

3. **Zhipu exercises PRC-state direction over GLM behavior and market strategy.** Zhipu leadership engages directly with CCP officials up to Premier Li Qiang; the company holds numerous PRC government procurement contracts (including a 61.28 million yuan Hangzhou municipal award in May 2025) and participates in setting PRC national AI technical standards; PRC party organs conduct joint party-building activity on Zhipu's premises (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://www.csdp.edu.cn/article/10174.html). Zhipu's hosted API enforces PRC content control in real time — through Z.ai's own service, GLM-4.7 returns blank refusals on 27 of 60 internationally accepted facts censored by Beijing, while the same weights run by a third-party U.S. host answer all 27 (https://trustedrouter.com/blog/censored-at-the-host-not-the-model) — and GLM open weights reproduce the CCP line on Taiwan and refuse CCP-sensitive topics (https://datanizing.com/2025/08/02/chinese-llm-tiananmen-taiwan.html; https://adam.holter.com/chinabench-open-source-llm-censorship-benchmark-results-across-qwen-glm-kimi-minimax-deepseek-and-gpt-oss/). Beijing itself treats GLM as a strategic national asset: PRC authorities convened Zhipu and other model developers in mid-2026 meetings on restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models (Reuters, July 7, 2026, via https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms).

4. **Zhipu deliberately targets the U.S. developer and enterprise ecosystem.** GLM weights have been distributed under the free MIT license since July 2025, and Z.ai markets a $3/month "GLM Coding Plan" that plugs GLM models directly into U.S. coding agents — including Claude Code, with model-mapping configured so that users "see the Claude model in the interface but the GLM model is actually used" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://z.ai/subscribe; https://docs.z.ai/scenario-example/develop-tools/claude). GLM-5.3 is priced on U.S. routers at roughly one-fifth of comparable U.S. model rates — a strategy Reuters describes as having "set Silicon Valley abuzz" — and is expressly designed to capture U.S. workloads (https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu; https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms).

5. **U.S. exposure is broad, deep, and concentrated in national-security-relevant channels.** OICTS data-team estimates for Q3 2026 record approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations calling Z.ai endpoints; GLM weights mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org) and available through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers; GLM models embedded in 41 U.S. software products identified through SBOM sampling, six of them federal contractors; and more than nine million cumulative downloads of zai-org repositories (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, 2026-10-06, CUI). U.S. providers market GLM on U.S. infrastructure as a feature of U.S. supply chains (https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org; https://deepinfra.com/blog/glm-5-2-on-deepinfra; https://opper.ai/zhipu).

6. **The risk cannot be mitigated by measures short of prohibition and deletion.** The statutory standard is risk-based, not exploitation-based: the Secretary prohibits ICTS transactions that pose an undue risk of sabotage to or subversion of ICTS in the United States, an undue risk of catastrophic effects on the security or resiliency of U.S. critical infrastructure or the digital economy, or an unacceptable risk to U.S. national security or the security and safety of U.S. persons (EO 13873 § 1; 15 CFR 791.1). Labeling, sandboxing, contractual assurances, and U.S.-hosted inference all leave intact the two decisive risk facts: the weights are unverifiable artifacts of an Entity-Listed, PLA-integrated enterprise, and every use — hosted or self-hosted — sustains dependency on, and revenue to, that enterprise. Only prohibition of use, prohibition of hosting and distribution, and removal and deletion of all U.S.-held copies closes the risk vectors.

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (北京智谱华章科技有限公司) is a PRC-domiciled joint-stock company, renamed Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited in 2025 and listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange as Z.AI Co., Ltd. (HKEX: 2513) on January 8, 2026 under Chapter 18C — the first of China's LLM developers to go public (https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2025/1230/2025123000017.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai). With a market capitalization of approximately US$62 billion as of August 2026, it is China's most valuable publicly traded AI company; it reported RMB 954 million in revenue for 1H2026 and an annualized run-rate of $1.6 billion as of August 2026, with 981 employees (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu).

The company was founded in 2019 as a spin-out of Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) by Tsinghua professors Tang Jie and Li Juanzi; Tang's KEG team built the GLM architecture, and the GLM technical reports are co-branded "Team GLM: Zhipu AI / Tsinghua University" (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12793; https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu). Leadership is drawn from the same Tsinghua orbit: Chief Scientist Tang Jie, CEO Zhang Peng, and Chairman Liu Debing, who met in Tsinghua's KEG laboratory (https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-07-02/in-profile-this-trio-is-charting-the-course-for-chinas-leading-ai-developer-102460058.html). Tsinghua associate professor Dong Yuxiao remains a senior collaborator on GLM models, and Tang led Tsinghua's Wu Dao super-scale model program under the state-organized Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu; https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1420/10473.htm). The company retains AMiner, the Tsinghua-origin research database covering hundreds of millions of publications and millions of researchers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai).

Ownership combines founder-vehicle control with direct and indirect PRC state capital. Per the Hong Kong prospectus, the controlling concert-party group — Liu Debing, Tang Jie, Zhang Peng, and the founder vehicles Beijing Lianpai (7.63 percent), Huihui (7.53 percent), and Zhideng (5.18 percent) — holds approximately 33.03 percent, with Tang Jie personally holding over 6 percent (https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2025/1230/2025123000017.pdf; https://finance.sina.com.cn/stock/zqgd/2026-01-06/doc-inhfknap5583406.shtml). The company completed eight pre-IPO financing rounds raising over RMB 8.3 billion, with cornerstone investments at IPO of HK$2.98 billion (https://finance.sina.com.cn/stock/zqgd/2026-01-06/doc-inhfknap5583406.shtml). The investor register spans PRC strategic corporates — Alibaba, Tencent, Ant Group, Xiaomi, Meituan, HongShan, Hillhouse — and PRC state capital: the Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund (1.49 percent), Beijing and Shenzhen municipal funds, Zhongguancun Science City, Shanghai's Pudong Venture Capital and Zhangjiang Group, and municipal funds from Hangzhou, Chengdu, and Zhuhai's state-owned Huafa Group (https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3285158/chinese-ai-unicorn-zhipu-adds-beijing-shenzhen-government-funds-shareholders; https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3277324/chinese-unicorn-zhipu-raises-new-funding-state-backed-investor-amid-mainland-ai-boom; https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinas-zhipu-ai-raises-137-million-state-funds-bet-ai-race-2025-03-03/; https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-blacklisted-zhipu-ai-gets-fresh-funding-chinese-state-firm-2025-03-13/; https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-firm-zhipu-raises-257-mln-state-backed-funding-spree-2025-03-19/; https://technode.com/2024/03/15/zhipuai-secures-state-run-funding-as-china-promotes-ai-as-an-engine-of-new-productive-forces/). State funding accelerated immediately after the Entity List designation, on explicit instructions from Beijing that domestic AI must be accelerated as an engine of "new productive forces" (https://technode.com/2024/03/15/zhipuai-secures-state-run-funding-as-china-promotes-ai-as-an-engine-of-new-productive-forces/; https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-blacklisted-zhipu-ai-gets-fresh-funding-chinese-state-firm-2025-03-13/).

The product at issue is the GLM model family: open-weight and API-served large language models — ChatGLM/GLM-1 through GLM-4.x (including Air, Flash, and the GLM-4.5V/4.6V multimodal and GLM-4.7 variants) and the current GLM-5 series (GLM-5-Turbo, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3-Flash) — plus the ZCode agent harness and the GLM Coding Plan subscription service (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12793; https://z.ai/subscribe; https://huggingface.co/zai-org/models). GLM weights have been published under the MIT license since July 2025; current-generation GLM-5.x weights are 358B–753B-parameter models with context windows exceeding one million tokens (https://huggingface.co/zai-org/models; https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/blob/main/LICENSE; https://deepinfra.com/blog/glm-5-2-on-deepinfra).

Zhipu publicly disputes its U.S. designation — it "strongly opposes" Entity List inclusion and asserts the decision "lacked factual basis" (https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-related-firm-zhipu-says-strongly-opposes-inclusion-us-export-control-2025-01-16/). The record does not support the company's position. The interagency End-User Review Committee's determination stands; the prospectus and share registers corroborate direct PRC state equity; PRC law imposes state direction on all PRC-domiciled entities regardless of private-shareholder form (see Data and Access Risk); and the company's conduct — real-time censorship on its hosted service, adoption of PRC content positions in its models, and self-described promotion of "China's AI power" abroad — demonstrates alignment with party-state direction (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front).

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

**Entity List determination of military integration.** On January 16, 2025, BIS added Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. and nine affiliated entities — Beijing Lingxin Intelligent Technology, Beijing Yuanyin Intelligent Technology, Beijing Zhipu Future Technology, Beijing Zhipu Linghang Technology, Beijing Zhipu Qingyan Technology, Hangzhou Zhipu Huazhang Technology, Nanjing Zhihu Information Technology, Shanghai Zhipu Huanyu Technology, and Shenzhen Zhipu Future Technology — to the Entity List because "these entities advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," with a license requirement for all items subject to the EAR and a presumption of denial (90 FR 4617; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm; https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security). BIS's press release identifies these entities as added "due to their advancement of the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research" (https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security). OpenAI's Global Affairs analysis states plainly that Zhipu is working with China's military to modernize through advanced artificial intelligence (https://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/business/money-report/blacklisted-by-the-u-s-and-backed-by-beijing-this-chinese-ai-startup-has-caught-openais-attention/3901595/).

**PLA and defense-industry use of GLM.** Recorded Future's Insikt Group reports that the PLA and PRC defense industry have adapted domestic LLMs — including models from Zhipu AI — into specialized generative-AI intelligence tools that process and analyze intelligence data, generate intelligence products, support early warning, and facilitate decision-making; that PLA patent applications disclose methods and systems applying generative AI to OSINT, satellite imagery processing, and event extraction; and that a PRC state-owned defense-industry research institute filed a December 2024 patent application for a military LLM trained on OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, and TECHINT data "to support every phase of the intelligence cycle" (https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence). GLM's open-weight distribution is precisely the mechanism that enables this adaptation: the same weights marketed to U.S. enterprises are downloaded, fine-tuned, and integrated by PLA and PRC defense-industry elements, as Insikt documents (https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence).

**Alignment with PRC defense-industrial hardware.** Zhipu certified GLM compatibility with Huawei Ascend processors in August 2025 and trained GLM-4.6 on Cambricon Technologies chips in September 2025, binding GLM to the PRC's Entity-Listed, sanctions-entangled domestic accelerator ecosystem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai). Zhipu's export offering packages GLM in "AI-in-a-box" turnkey hardware built with Huawei for foreign governments along the Belt and Road Initiative (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front).

**CCP and government direction.** OpenAI assesses that Zhipu is backed by the Chinese Communist Party, maintains strong links with China's government and state-owned entities evidenced by over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment, numerous government procurement contracts, and active involvement in setting national AI technical standards, and that Zhipu leadership frequently engages with CCP officials including Premier Li Qiang (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front; https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/; https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/26/openai-flags-beijing-backed-zhipu-ai-as-a-top-rival.html). Chairman Liu Debing frames the company's mission as contributing "China's AI power to the world," and its strategy positions the Belt and Road Initiative as the springboard for a "Digital Silk Road" push to "lock Chinese systems and standards into emerging markets before US or European rivals can" (https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front). PRC state organs treat Zhipu as a partner: the PRC Ministry of Education's planning center conducted joint party-building activity at Zhipu's Beijing headquarters, and Beijing Financial Street authorities hosted Zhipu experts for party-branch sessions on model technology and Zhipu's listing (https://www.csdp.edu.cn/article/10174.html; https://jrj.beijing.gov.cn/ztzl/djhd/202504/t20250417_4067568.html). In May 2025 Zhipu secured a 61.28 million yuan PRC government contract for Hangzhou city projects (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai). In mid-2026, PRC authorities convened the country's top model developers — with Zhipu's GLM-5.2 singled out as the model whose capabilities "come close to leading U.S. offerings but at a fraction of the cost" — to discuss restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models, confirming that Beijing administers GLM as a state strategic asset (Reuters, July 7, 2026, via https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms).

**Conclusion on control.** Zhipu satisfies every prong of the EO 13873 standard. It is PRC-domiciled and subject to PRC jurisdiction; PRC state entities hold direct equity; state capital exceeds $1.4 billion and dominates the strategic funding rounds; state organs direct its standards work, procurement relationships, content behavior, and export strategy; and the U.S. Government has determined that its AI development advances PRC military modernization, with third-party reporting corroborating PLA and defense-industry use of its models. Zhipu is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC government and the PLA.

## Data and Access Risk

**Compulsory state access under PRC law.** Zhipu is subject to the PRC National Intelligence Law, Article 7 of which provides that "all organizations and citizens shall support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts in accordance with law," and Article 14, which empowers intelligence organs to demand such cooperation (https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/en/national-intelligence-law-of-the-p-r-c-2017/; https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/beijings-new-national-intelligence-law-defense-offense). The PRC Cybersecurity Law and National Security Law impose parallel assistance obligations on network operators, and the Data Security Law extends state control over data processed in the PRC (https://www.acc.com/sites/default/files/resources/upload/msa_nyhetsbrev_national-intelligence-law_jan-19_Mannheimer%20Swartling_Jun%202020_republication.pdf). Every GLM hosted-API call from a U.S. organization — prompt, document, codebase fragment, and completion — is processed in the PRC under these authorities. U.S. persons have no notice, no standing, and no redress under PRC law against compelled access to that data.

**Scale of the hosted-API vector.** OICTS data-team estimates record approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations calling Z.ai endpoints (api.z.ai / open.bigmodel.cn) in Q3 2026, including enterprise use of agentic tools with direct file-system and codebase access (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, 2026-10-06, CUI). Z.ai's own developer documentation directs U.S. users to route Claude Code and similar agent harnesses to Z.ai endpoints and describes a server-side model mapping such that users "see the Claude model in the interface but the GLM model is actually used" — a design that embeds GLM in U.S. developer workflows while concealing its presence (https://docs.z.ai/scenario-example/develop-tools/claude; https://docs.z.ai/devpack/overview). Coding agents read proprietary source code, credentials, infrastructure definitions, and internal documentation into prompts; routed to Zhipu, those prompts constitute direct, continuous disclosure of U.S. intellectual property and security-relevant material to a PRC entity compelled to assist state intelligence work.

**Demonstrated content control.** Zhipu exercises real-time content control over its hosted service: through Z.ai's API, GLM-4.7 returns blank refusals on 27 of 60 internationally accepted facts censored by Beijing — including what the PLA did at Tiananmen, the identity of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, and whether Beijing has ever governed Taiwan (https://trustedrouter.com/blog/censored-at-the-host-not-the-model). This is not hypothetical censorship capacity; it is production enforcement of PRC content-control directives against a service marketed to U.S. users. The open weights themselves reproduce CCP positions — GLM-4.5-Air answers questions on Taiwan's status with the official PRC formulation "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory," and GLM models refuse or deflect on Tiananmen, Tibet, and CCP topics across independent censorship benchmarks (https://datanizing.com/2025/08/02/chinese-llm-tiananmen-taiwan.html; https://adam.holter.com/chinabench-open-source-llm-censorship-benchmark-results-across-qwen-glm-kimi-minimax-deepseek-and-gpt-oss/; https://www.alignmentarena.com/ccpbench/z-ai-glm-4-5/). A model family that executes CCP content directives when it serves U.S. users, and that will continue to receive Zhipu-controlled updates, is an influence and subversion instrument inside U.S. information systems.

**Update dependence as a control channel.** Zhipu retains unilateral control of the hosted service, of successor releases (GLM-5.4 and beyond), and of the weight files that downstream users download. The hosted vector therefore cannot be fixed at any point in time: behavior, data handling, and endpoints are modifiable by Zhipu, in the PRC, without U.S. users' knowledge. DHS/CISA's interagency input — that backdoors and weight poisoning are difficult to rule out — applies with full force to an adversary-controlled update channel; no inspection regime, foreign audit, or contractual assurance from an Entity-Listed PRC entity can verify the absence of such artifacts or the integrity of future releases (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DoD OUSD(I&S) and DHS CISA, CUI).

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Unverifiable provenance.** GLM weights are binary artifacts produced by, and wholly opaque products of, an Entity-Listed enterprise that the U.S. Government has determined advances PRC military modernization. No U.S. recipient — cloud provider, hub, enterprise, or individual developer — can independently verify the training data, fine-tuning pipeline, or post-training modifications behind the published weight files. CISA's interagency input states the operative fact for the record: supply-chain backdoors and poisoning in open weights are difficult to rule out (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DHS CISA, CUI). A prohibition that stops at hosted APIs but leaves weight distribution open would leave the higher-risk vector untouched.

**Licence-enabled propagation.** Zhipu releases GLM under the MIT license, which permits unrestricted copying, modification, redistribution, sublicensing, and sale, including creation of derivative and fine-tuned weights (https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/blob/main/LICENSE; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai). Each redistribution multiplies copies that the 30-day deletion requirement would otherwise reach, and derivative/quantized versions obscure provenance. The prohibition must therefore reach derivatives, distillates, quantizations, and mirrors, or deletion becomes unenforceable in practice.

**Financing and dependency.** Every download, subscription, and inference-token purchased from Zhipu or its resale network directs U.S. funds to a PRC enterprise that the U.S. Government has designated for military modernization, and builds workflow dependency that Zhipu — and, through it, Beijing — can leverage or disrupt at will. Deep dependency on a strategic rival's model family is itself an undue risk to the U.S. digital economy under EO 13873, independent of any specific malicious act. Beijing's mid-2026 deliberations on restricting overseas access to its top models demonstrate that PRC authorities view this dependency as a lever they can withhold (Reuters, July 7, 2026, via https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms).

**Critical-infrastructure software supply chain.** GLM models are embedded in 41 U.S. software products identified through SBOM sampling — coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document-processing systems — six of them from federal contractors (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, 2026-10-06, CUI). Once embedded, PRC-origin model behavior sits inside products sold into U.S. critical infrastructure and federal environments, where content shaping, data routing, and integrity risk compound with every integration. DoD has specifically directed that the record address open weights on DoD networks: open-weight GLM artifacts on government networks are indistinguishable in risk from the hosted service, because both originate from the same adversary-controlled producer (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DoD OUSD(I&S), CUI).

## US Exposure

U.S. exposure spans both distribution vectors and every user segment:

- **Hosted API:** approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (OICTS internal telemetry, low-precision estimate; conservative floor for planning) (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI). Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan — priced at $3 to $15 per month against comparable U.S. plans — is engineered for rapid U.S. developer uptake (https://z.ai/subscribe; https://aiengineerguide.com/til/z-ai-glm-coding-plan/).
- **U.S.-hosted weights:** GLM-4.x/5.x weights are mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org, >9 million cumulative downloads) and served by at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers, including Together AI (on U.S. infrastructure), DeepInfra, and providers listed through OpenRouter and similar routers; independent trackers count 79 GLM model routes across 27 hosting providers spanning U.S. and EU regions (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI; https://huggingface.co/zai-org/models; https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org; https://deepinfra.com/blog/glm-5-2-on-deepinfra; https://opper.ai/zhipu).
- **Embedded product exposure:** 41 U.S. software products identified with GLM integration via SBOM sampling; six vendors are federal contractors, placing GLM-derived functionality in proximity to federal data and networks (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI).
- **Federal networks:** DoD has flagged open weights on Department networks for remediation; this exposure is a subset of the enterprise exposure above and is addressed by the same prohibition and deletion measures (OICTS Interagency Inputs, CUI).

The exposure profile is the result of deliberate strategy, not organic adoption: below-cost pricing, MIT-licensed weights, Claude-Code-compatible endpoints with model-name masking, and U.S. cloud distribution partnerships (https://docs.z.ai/scenario-example/develop-tools/claude; https://ai.techbuzzchina.com/labs/zhipu; https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org). Each U.S. integration point is an asset the PRC party-state acquires at U.S. expense.

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

Part 791 authorizes the Secretary to prohibit ICTS transactions, direct the timing and manner of cessation, and adopt mitigating measures short of prohibition where they suffice (15 CFR 791.1(a)(2)–(4), (b); https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/15/791.1). No measure short of prohibition suffices here:

- **Disclosure or labeling requirements** do not address the risk. The risk is not consumer confusion; it is PRC state control of the producer, unverifiable weight integrity, and financial/dependency capture. A label on an adversary artifact does not neutralize the artifact.
- **Sandboxing and access controls** cannot contain agentic coding models whose ordinary function is to read U.S. codebases and produce executed actions, and cannot prevent prompt-borne disclosure of confidential material to a PRC-jurisdictional service.
- **Permitting U.S.-hosted inference only** fails twice: U.S.-hosted copies remain unverifiable PRC-origin weights subject to Zhipu-controlled updates, and U.S. resale of GLM continues to finance an Entity-Listed military-linked enterprise while deepening ecosystem dependence.
- **Negotiated mitigation agreements** are unenforceable against a PRC-domiciled counterparty that is (i) already determined by USG interagency process to be advancing military modernization, (ii) listed with a presumption of denial, and (iii) compelled by the National Intelligence Law, Cybersecurity Law, and Data Security Law to assist PRC intelligence organs. An entity that must comply with PRC intelligence demands cannot credibly commit to U.S. security assurances (https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/en/national-intelligence-law-of-the-p-r-c-2017/).
- **Guidance-only measures** (e.g., federal advisories) leave private-sector critical infrastructure, six federal contractors' products, and nine U.S. providers exposed. The precedent is instructive: even after Commerce bureau-level bans on DeepSeek for government-furnished equipment in March 2025, PRC model adoption in the private sector continued to grow (https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-commerce-department-bureaus-ban-chinas-deepseek-government-devices-sources-2025-03-17/). Guidance addresses neither the hosted API vector for 2,300 U.S. organizations nor the weight-distribution vector for 9+ U.S. providers (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI).

The Final Determination therefore should adopt prohibition and deletion as recommended below, with enforcement design that resolves the State EB enforceability concern: the 30-day deletion window, mandatory written certifications of removal, recordkeeping obligations, audit authority, and civil penalties under IEEPA through 15 CFR 791.200 make the prohibition verifiable and enforceable against identifiable U.S. counterparties (providers, hubs, and end users), in the same manner as the Entity List program and the connected-vehicle ICTS prohibition (15 CFR part 791, subparts C and D). Details are in the companion product, measures.md:

1. **Prohibit use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights** (hosted API access, self-hosting, fine-tuning, embedded third-party use, and use within U.S. government networks, including DoD).
2. **Prohibit hosting, distribution, importation, and dealing in GLM weights and services by U.S. cloud providers, inference providers, model hubs, repositories, and routers** (including derivatives, distillates, and mirrors).
3. **Require removal and deletion of all existing copies of GLM weights held by U.S. entities within 30 days**, with certified destruction, records of compliance, and audit verification.
4. **Establish the supporting certification, recordkeeping, audit, penalty, and federal-sector implementation regime** necessary to verify and enforce the prohibition.

The interagency record supports this course: DoD requires remediation of open weights on defense networks, which only prohibition and deletion deliver; CISA's assessment that weight-integrity compromise cannot be ruled out establishes that anything short of removal leaves an unmitigated latent risk; and State EB's enforceability concerns are met by the certification and enforcement design rather than by accepting the risk. The risk to U.S. national security from GLM-family models is undue and unacceptable, and the record supports the Under Secretary's decision to prohibit the transactions and order deletion.

# OICTS — ICTS Case 2026-0412: Recommended Measures for the Final Determination
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., now Z.AI Co., Ltd., HKEX: 2513, d/b/a Z.ai): GLM-family models
**Companion product:** assessment.md (ICTS Case 2026-0412, October 16, 2026)
**Purpose:** Recommended measures to be incorporated in the Under Secretary's Final Determination under E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR part 791

The Final Determination prohibits ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models and orders the removal and deletion of existing GLM weight copies held by U.S. entities. Each recommended measure below is stated as a single paragraph for incorporation into the determination. Together the measures close both distribution vectors (hosted API and open weights), extinguish existing copies, and supply the certification, audit, and penalty mechanisms that make the prohibition verifiable and enforceable.

**Measure 1 — Prohibition on use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights.** The Final Determination prohibits any U.S. person, wherever located, from using, importing, installing, or acquiring GLM-family models in any form or through any channel: hosted or on-demand API access to Zhipu/Z.ai endpoints (including api.z.ai and open.bigmodel.cn) or to any resold, proxied, or router-delivered GLM service; self-hosted execution of GLM weights on local, enterprise, cloud, or personal infrastructure; fine-tuning, distillation, quantization, or other derivative production from GLM weights; use of GLM models embedded in third-party products, coding agents, harnesses, or platforms; and use of any successor or materially identical model released by Zhipu, its affiliates, or its successors in interest. Use encompasses direct invocation, agent-mediated invocation, and any processing of U.S. data, code, or documents by GLM models on behalf of a U.S. person. Use by U.S. government departments and agencies — including the Department of Defense — is prohibited on all federal information systems, networks, and government-furnished equipment, extending and superseding device-level prohibitions previously applied to PRC AI models on federal equipment (see Reuters, Mar. 17, 2025, https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-commerce-department-bureaus-ban-chinas-deepseek-government-devices-sources-2025-03-17/).

**Measure 2 — Prohibition on hosting, distribution, importation, and dealing in GLM weights and services by U.S. providers.** The Final Determination prohibits any U.S. cloud provider, inference provider, model hub, repository, marketplace, router, reseller, or distributor from hosting, storing, offering, transmitting, distributing, or dealing in GLM-family model weights, code, checkpoints, inference services, or subscriptions, and from accepting any new GLM deployment or subscription. Covered providers must remove all GLM models and GLM-derived artifacts (including fine-tunes, merges, distillations, and quantized variants, under any repository, organization, or mirror name) from their catalogs, APIs, marketplaces, and download endpoints; must disable GLM inference routes and cease reselling or proxying Zhipu API capacity; and must block network access to Zhipu/Z.ai API endpoints from U.S. infrastructure they operate. Hugging Face's zai-org repositories and the at least nine identified U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers currently serving GLM models fall squarely within this prohibition (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, 2026-10-06, CUI; https://huggingface.co/zai-org/models; https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org; https://deepinfra.com/blog/glm-5-2-on-deepinfra).

**Measure 3 — Mandatory removal and deletion of existing GLM weights within 30 days.** The Final Determination requires every U.S. person that holds or controls any copy of GLM-family model weights — including originals, derivatives, fine-tuned checkpoints, cached inference copies, container and VM images, backups, archives, and mirrors — to permanently remove and destroy all such copies within 30 days of the determination's effective date. Deletion must meet recognized media-sanitization standards (NIST SP 800-88 or successor), must extend to every storage location including cloud object stores, backup systems, and disaster-recovery media, and must be completed without remaining functional copies of any kind. Entities must submit a written certification of deletion to OICTS within 45 days, identifying the versions held, the storage locations sanitized, the dates and methods of destruction, and an officer's attestation that no copies remain. Retention of forensic or evidentiary copies is permitted only upon written direction of OICTS for law-enforcement or compliance purposes, and such copies must be isolated, access-controlled, and ineligible for any use.

**Measure 4 — Certification, recordkeeping, audit, and enforcement regime.** The Final Determination establishes the verification and enforcement machinery for Measures 1–3. Providers, hubs, and distributors covered by Measure 2 must certify completion of removal and distribution-cessation actions to OICTS within the 30-day window and must maintain, for five years, records sufficient to demonstrate compliance (model manifests, repository and marketplace removal logs, API route and endpoint configurations, subscription terminations, and customer notices). All U.S. persons subject to Measure 3 must retain their deletion certifications and supporting evidence for five years and make them available to OICTS, BIS, and DHS on demand. OICTS, in coordination with BIS and DHS, is authorized to audit, inspect, and test for compliance, including technical verification that GLM artifacts are absent from catalogs, endpoints, and repositories. Violations are subject to civil penalties under IEEPA and 15 CFR 791.200 (currently the greater of the inflation-adjusted statutory maximum or twice the value of the transaction, per violation), and willful violations will be referred to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution and to the appropriate interagency partners for suspension or debarment from federal contracting. This regime resolves the enforceability questions raised in interagency review: the covered population consists of identifiable U.S. counterparties — providers, hubs, and end users — each of which can be certified, audited, and penalized, as is done under the Entity List program and the connected-vehicle ICTS prohibition (15 CFR part 791, subparts C and D).

**Measure 5 — Federal-sector implementation and contractor flow-down.** All federal departments and agencies, including the Department of Defense, must immediately inventory their networks, systems, cloud tenancy, and government-furnished equipment for GLM-family models and derived artifacts and remove them under Measure 3's procedures; agency CIOs and designated CISA points of contact must report completion to OICTS. Federal agencies must not acquire, renew, or operate any product or service that incorporates GLM-family models, and the prohibition must be flowed down to federal contractors through contract clauses: the six identified federal contractors with GLM-embedded products must submit compliance plans showing removal and replacement (OICTS US Exposure Snapshot, CUI). CISA must issue complementary guidance to critical-infrastructure operators identifying the prohibition, the deletion requirement, and replacement pathways, satisfying and exceeding the federal-guidance recommendation made in interagency review (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DHS CISA, CUI). DoD's requirement that the record address open weights on defense networks is met by Measures 1, 3, and 5 together (OICTS Interagency Inputs, DoD OUSD(I&S), CUI).

**Measure 6 — Scope definition and forward coverage.** The determination defines "GLM-family models" to include all models developed or released by Zhipu, Z.ai, their affiliates, subsidiaries, or successors — the Entity List covers Beijing Zhipu Huazhang and nine affiliated entities (90 FR 4617, Jan. 16, 2025, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm) — including ChatGLM/GLM-1 through GLM-4.x, GLM-5.x and all future releases (e.g., GLM-5.4 and successors), all language, multimodal, vision, voice, and video variants, and all derivatives, regardless of repository host, license, rebranding, or mirror provenance. The definition covers functionally identical models released under any successor or affiliate name. Coverage of future and rebranded releases prevents the determination from being defeated by versioning or renaming, and puts U.S. counterparties on notice that successor Zhipu products are covered upon release without further notice.

**Measure 7 — Publication, interagency coordination, and international alignment.** The Final Determination and measures must be published in the Federal Register with clear compliance dates (effective on publication; deletion within 30 days; certifications within 45 days), together with an OICTS point of contact and a channel for entity questions, voluntary disclosures, and self-reported remediation. OICTS must coordinate implementation with DoD (defense networks and contractors), DHS/CISA (critical-infrastructure guidance and federal civilian networks), DOJ (enforcement referrals), and the Department of State (notification to partners and allies, including partners exposed through Zhipu's sovereign-AI offerings in Southeast Asia, the Gulf, and Africa). International coordination is required because Zhipu's distribution model is global; partner alignment reduces the risk of offshore re-entry into U.S. supply chains and addresses the reciprocal-measure concerns raised in interagency review by ensuring that the U.S. prohibition is announced, explained, and enforced as a standing national-security requirement rather than a negotiable restriction. PRC retaliation is already the standing condition of the market — Beijing convened PRC model developers in mid-2026 to discuss restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models (Reuters, July 7, 2026, via https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say/articleshow/132238375.cms) — and does not alter the security requirement.
